name: Halversen & Co. Handknit Wool-Analog Sweater
description:
Halversen & Co. occupies a strange position in Meridian 88's fashion ecosystem: a Tier 5 label that sells hand-finished knitwear that looks, at first glance, like something a grandmother made. The sweaters are produced by a cooperative of master knitters working in small batches — each piece has visible evidence of human hands in the work, slight irregularities in the tension that machine production can't replicate. The wool-analog fiber is exceptionally fine, derived from a bioengineered fiber that mimics the warmth and softness of Shetland wool without any of its variability. This particular model is a boxy, slightly oversized crew-neck in a natural undyed cream, with a textured cable-knit front panel and ribbed sleeves.

The people who buy Halversen & Co. are not showing off — or rather, they're showing off in a way that only other people who know will understand. The sweater costs more than most Tier 2 workers earn in a month. It looks like something you could find at a secondhand market. That tension is entirely deliberate.
what_it_says: Wealth expressed through restraint — someone so secure in their position they don't need to signal it loudly. Or someone performing that security.
worn_by: Spire residents with old-money aesthetic sensibilities
senior executives who dress deliberately down
story_hooks: One of Halversen's master knitters has been embedding tiny irregularities in the cable patterns that function as a personal cipher — every sweater she's made in the last three years contains a message.

A Halversen sweater was found in a Shelf charity donation — still in its original wrapping, never worn, with a handwritten note inside that names a Tier 5 resident in connection with something serious.

Halversen & Co.'s cooperative is facing a quiet hostile acquisition by a Tier 5 conglomerate that wants the brand name but intends to automate production — the knitters are looking for someone to help them fight it.
